note: Beatrice is speaking. At the end of Canto 4 her eyes shone so brightly that Dante had to look away, and she now explains why.
A rule of Dante's Heaven: love follows sight. The more clearly a soul sees God, the more it loves, and the more it shines.

quote: only a trace of this same light
note: Whatever people love on earth, they love because some reflection of God's goodness shows in it. The mistake is to take the reflection for the source. Virgil taught the same in Purgatorio 17–18.
The question Dante asked at the end of Canto 4: can a broken vow be made up for by a different good deed?

context: Her lesson on vows fills the first half of the canto.

note: Dante steps outside the story for a moment and speaks of his poem as a poem, divided into cantos.

The conviction at the center of the whole poem. Without free will there could be no merit and no blame, and so no justice in Hell, Purgatory or Heaven. Dante says the same in his treatise on monarchy, where he calls freedom God's greatest gift to human nature.
Angels and human beings, and no others.
A true vow is a promise of something that God accepts. A promise to do something foolish or wrong is no vow, as the examples below will show.
In making a vow a person freely gives up his freedom in that matter. Since nothing he has is worth more than his free will, nothing he could offer in its place would be enough.
What was vowed already belongs to God. To put it to some other good use is like giving alms with stolen money.
The Church did release people from vows, or let them swap one for another. That seems to contradict what Beatrice has just proved.
Teaching as food, an image Dante loves: Canto 2 spoke of the bread of angels, and he named his book of philosophy the Convivio, the banquet.
The thing promised (a fast, a pilgrimage, a life of chastity) and the promise itself, the compact with God.

quote: The agreement can never be canceled
note: The promise binds until it is kept. Only the thing promised can ever be changed.
The Law of Moses required offerings to be made, but allowed some things that had been vowed to be redeemed or exchanged for something else (Leviticus 27).

The keys of Saint Peter, which the angel at the gate of Purgatory holds (Purgatorio 9): gold for the Church's power to absolve, silver for the judgment needed to use it. No one may change his own vow. It takes the authority of the Church.

quote: as four is contained in six
note: The new offering must be worth more than the old, half as much again.

A vow that gives the whole self, like a nun's vow of chastity. Nothing outweighs it, so nothing can be put in its place. This is the answer to Piccarda's case, and it is stricter than many church lawyers of Dante's day, who held that a pope could release from any vow.
A judge of Israel who vowed that if God gave him victory he would sacrifice whatever first came out of his house to meet him. It was his only daughter, and he kept the vow (Judges 11).

Agamemnon, leader of the Greeks against Troy. When the fleet lay becalmed at Aulis he sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to the goddess Diana. In the version Dante knew from Cicero, he had vowed to offer the most beautiful thing born in his kingdom that year, and it was she.
Beatrice turns from Dante to address all Christians, in the tone of a sermon.
Usually read as a warning against vows made lightly to win God's favor, or against the easy releases from vows that some clergy handed out.
The pope. Scripture and the Church's guidance are enough to save a soul. No one needs to load himself with extra vows.
The Jews who lived in Christian cities kept their own Law with care. They would have good reason to laugh at Christians who treat a vow as a trifle.
The Christian who leaves the nourishment of Scripture and the Church to follow his own whims, and only harms himself.

quote: where the world is most alive
note: Upward, toward the light. Commentators differ on whether Dante means the sun, the equator of the heavens, where they turn fastest, or the Empyrean.
As in Canto 2, the climb from one heaven to the next takes no time at all.

quote: the planet itself grew more radiant
note: Beatrice's joy adds light to the planet. The heavenly bodies were held to be changeless, so this is a marvel.
If even an unchanging star can be changed by her smile, how much more a human being, whose nature is to change.

quote: As fish in a clear, peaceful pond
note: A well-loved simile. The souls swim up to Dante as fish rise to anything that might be food: he is a new occasion for love.
The souls of Mercury. In the moon Dante saw faint faces. Here he sees lights, though he can still just make out a figure inside each one.

Dante's Italian says only "here is one who", and most readers take the souls to mean Dante himself, a newcomer to love. Love in Heaven is not divided by being shared: it grows with every soul there is to love.
One of the poem's direct addresses to the reader. Dante teases: imagine if I stopped here.
Heaven is the Church Triumphant, its battle won. The Church on earth was called the Church Militant, still at war with sin, which is why life here is a battle.

context: He is not named until Canto 6, which he speaks from its first line to its last.

note: The blessed share in God's own nature. Boethius, a philosopher Dante revered, wrote that everyone who is truly happy is a god, though God is one.
The soul is wrapped in the light that its own joy gives off, like a bird in its nest. The light comes from its eyes and grows when it smiles.
Mercury is so close to the sun that it is usually lost in the sun's glare.
When the sun burns off the morning haze it becomes too bright to look at. The soul's joy at being asked makes it shine so strongly that its figure disappears inside its own light.
Canto 6 is the only canto of the poem spoken entirely by one character.
